title: YOUR SPOUSE’S BODY IS NOT YOUR PROPERTY: WHAT 1 CORINTHIANS 7 ACTUALLY SAYS ABOUT SEXUAL AUTHORITY
paragraphs:
YOUR SPOUSE’S BODY IS NOT YOUR PROPERTY: WHAT 1 CORINTHIANS 7 ACTUALLY SAYS ABOUT SEXUAL AUTHORITY
One of the Bible’s most intimate passages has been used to demand sex, excuse rejection, shame wounded spouses, and defend selfishness. But when you actually read Paul’s words carefully, something breathtaking appears: Christian marriage was never supposed to be a battle over who gets control. It was supposed to become a place where two people learn what Christlike self-giving love costs.
There is a sentence in the Bible that can sound terrifying in the hands of the wrong person.
“The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband…”
Stop there, and someone can build a weapon out of Scripture.
But Paul did not stop there.
“…and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife.”
Because whatever interpretation you give the first half must survive the second.

Paul does not hand the husband a throne while placing the wife beneath it. He does something astonishingly reciprocal. He takes the language of authority and places husband and wife beneath the same obligation of self-giving.
And perhaps some marriages desperately need to hear that.
Because somewhere tonight, one spouse feels rejected.
Someone is lying inches away from the person they married while emotionally feeling a thousand miles apart.
Someone has been told, “The Bible says you have to.”
Someone else has weaponized exhaustion, resentment, silence, or sexual withdrawal.
Someone desperately wants affection but is ashamed to admit it.
Someone dreads being touched because intimacy stopped feeling like tenderness and started feeling like an obligation they were never allowed to discuss.
And somewhere, two Christians love Jesus deeply but have never learned how to talk honestly about sex without embarrassment, defensiveness, guilt, accusation, or fear.
Not to hand one spouse ammunition against the other.
Not to transform the marriage bed into a courtroom.
But to confront selfishness on both sides.
The Greek underneath these words makes the reciprocity difficult to escape.
ἡ γυνὴ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει
hē gynē tou idiou sōmatos ouk exousiazei
ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει
homoios de kai ho anēr tou idiou sōmatos ouk exousiazei
The crucial verb is ἐξουσιάζει—exousiazei—from ἐξουσιάζω, carrying the idea of exercising authority or having authority over something.
And Paul deliberately applies it both ways.
The wife does not possess unilateral sexual authority within marriage.
That is why this passage cannot honestly be reduced to, “My spouse owes me sex whenever I demand it.”
The very structure of Paul’s argument destroys unilateralism.
The person quoting verse 4 to establish his or her authority over a spouse must confront the fact that Paul simultaneously limits that person's independent authority too.
“Your body belongs to me, therefore I control you.”
“I entered a covenant in which my sexuality is no longer something I approach as though only my desires, preferences, frustrations, vulnerabilities, and needs matter.”
“Let the husband render unto the wife due benevolence: and likewise also the wife unto the husband.”
The noun opheilē carries the idea of something owed or due, while apodidōmi means to give, render, or pay what is due.
Paul therefore does teach genuine marital obligation.
We should not soften Scripture until it says nothing uncomfortable.
Marriage involves sexual responsibility toward one's spouse.
But neither should we harden Scripture into something Paul did not say.
And when Paul addresses temporary abstinence, the decision is mutual.
It comes from the idea of agreement or harmony. It is related to the word from which English gets “symphony.”
Not one spouse quoting Scripture until the other submits from fear.
Paul envisions even temporary sexual abstinence for prayer as something husband and wife agree upon together.
So there are two opposite distortions we must refuse.
The first says, “My body is mine, my sexuality concerns only me, and marriage places no meaningful sexual responsibility upon me.”
But the second says, “Your body belongs to me, therefore I may demand access regardless of your fear, pain, trauma, exhaustion, illness, emotional condition, or willingness.”
Paul's reciprocal language does not establish that either.
Biblical mutual authority is not permission for coercion.
Sexual coercion is not transformed into holiness because somebody attached a Bible verse to it.
If your spouse is frightened of you, something is wrong.
If your spouse has learned that saying “not tonight” will produce rage, intimidation, humiliation, threats, punishment, or spiritual condemnation, something is wrong.
If Scripture is being used to silence pain instead of shepherding the hurting person toward safety, truth, healing, and Christ, something is wrong.
And if you have experienced sexual coercion or abuse, this passage should never be used to tell you that abuse was God's design for marriage.
Yet there is another person reading this who needs conviction from the opposite direction.
Maybe your marriage is physically safe.
You discovered that withholding affection could hurt your spouse, so eventually intimacy became leverage.
The bedroom becomes a graveyard where both people pretend nothing died.
Other translations render the thought as not depriving one another.
This passage keeps refusing to let either spouse become the center.
That is because Christian marriage is supposed to be shaped by something larger than sexual appetite.
“For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.”
Christ did not love by asking only:
And Christian marriage slowly crucifies the selfish instinct that constantly asks:
Sometimes selflessness means lovingly giving yourself to your spouse when laziness would rather withdraw.
Sometimes selflessness means hearing your spouse say, “I am hurting,” and caring more about that person than about immediate gratification.
Sometimes love asks, “Have I made you feel unwanted?”
And sometimes love has enough courage to ask an even more painful question:
That conversation may reveal wounds nobody expected.
Past sexual trauma can follow someone into a marriage bed long after the event itself ended.
Emotional abandonment can make physical intimacy extraordinarily difficult.
And unresolved bitterness can turn two bodies that once reached for each other instinctively into strangers.
This is where simplistic Christian slogans can do terrible damage.
Sometimes the most biblical thing a couple can do is finally tell the truth.
Because biblical intimacy is not merely bodies occupying the same bed.
It involves covenant faithfulness, tenderness, honesty, repentance, patience, sacrifice, and love.
Paul had already written only a few verses earlier:
“Know ye not that your bodies are the members of Christ?”
Your body ultimately belongs to Christ.
Your spouse's body ultimately belongs to Christ.
That should put holy fear into every discussion of sexual authority.
Because you are not handling property.
You are loving someone for whom Christ died.
Someone whose vulnerabilities you were trusted to protect.
And perhaps this is where the passage becomes unbearably personal.
What if the biggest problem in your marriage is not frequency?
What if the argument about sex is only revealing something underneath it?
“I feel like you only touch me when you want something.”
“I feel rejected every time I reach for you.”
“I don't know how to tell you what happened to me.”
“I am scared that if I tell you the truth, you won't understand.”
Suddenly this is not merely a theological debate.
There are human beings underneath the doctrine.
There is a husband wondering why his wife no longer reaches for him.
There is a wife quietly wondering whether her husband still finds her beautiful.

There is the couple whose baby finally fell asleep, whose bills are overdue, whose bodies are exhausted, whose patience is disappearing, and who cannot remember the last time they looked at one another without discussing chores.
There is the marriage damaged by pornography.
The marriage where rejection has accumulated for so long that neither person knows how to initiate without fear.
And Jesus walks into those places too.
This is why Christian sexual ethics cannot ultimately be reduced to “Who has rights?”
At the center of Christianity stands a Savior who laid down His life.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
That is radically different from using Scripture to demand that another person serve your appetite.
And wives are not called to manipulate, humiliate, punish, or casually neglect their husbands either.
Christian marriage confronts selfishness wherever it hides.
Because sin loves to turn gifts into weapons.
But entitlement can poison desire until intimacy begins to feel like extraction rather than communion.
Maybe the question your marriage needs tonight is not:
“How often are we supposed to have sex?”
“I don't want you afraid to tell me when you're hurting.”
“I didn't realize how deeply my constant rejection was affecting you.”
“I let pornography reshape what I expected from you.”
Because Christianity does not begin with pretending we have no sin.
It begins with bringing sin into the light.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Maybe your marriage cannot be repaired by another argument over 1 Corinthians 7.
No “I'm sorry you felt that way.”
No Bible verses thrown like grenades.
Because this is what Jesus does.
He takes sinners whose desires became disordered, whose marriages became wounded, whose histories became complicated, whose choices became shameful…
and He does not merely expose them.
The Gospel does not say your worst chapter must become your final chapter.
The Samaritan woman's relational history was exposed in conversation with Jesus.
The woman caught in adultery stood publicly disgraced.
Not by pretending sin was harmless.
By confronting sin and pouring grace upon repentant sinners.
That is the difference between cheap affirmation and Gospel grace.
“You do not have to remain what sin has made you.”
So if you have pressured your spouse, repent.
If you have intentionally weaponized rejection, repent.
If pornography has entered your marriage, bring it into the light and seek help.
If adultery shattered trust, stop demanding instant restoration and begin walking the long road of truthful repentance.
If trauma is affecting intimacy, there is no shame in seeking wise, trauma-informed pastoral and professional help.
If physical pain is involved, appropriate medical care may matter.
If abuse or coercion is occurring, safety matters. Seeking outside help is not spiritual failure.
And if you and your spouse simply became distant somewhere between careers, children, dishes, bills, disappointments, and exhaustion…
Ask questions without preparing your defense while the other person answers.
Tell the truth without using truth as a weapon.
Forgive where genuine repentance is occurring.
Rebuild trust where trust was damaged.
Because the goal of Christian marriage was never merely sexual access.
It is covenant love shaped increasingly by Christ.
And suddenly Paul's seemingly shocking statement begins to look different.
“The wife hath not power of her own body…”
“…and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body…”
There is no isolated sovereign ego in Christian marriage saying:
And both belong first to Jesus.
So tonight, before quoting 1 Corinthians 7 at your spouse, perhaps place yourself underneath it first.
Ask what it requires of you.
Not merely what it requires of them.
That is where Scripture becomes a mirror instead of a weapon.
And perhaps you felt something while reading this that you were not expecting.
If you need healing, begin seeking it.
If you need help, reach for trustworthy help.
If you need to have a conversation with your spouse, perhaps tonight is the night you stop pretending everything is fine.
And if this exposed something hidden in you, comment, “Jesus, change my heart.”
If your marriage needs prayer, comment, “Pray for us.”
If Christ is restoring something you thought was dead, comment, “Jesus is still healing us.”
You never know who will read your words and realize they are not the only Christian struggling behind a smiling family photograph.

Not because every sentence will be easy to accept, but because there may come a night when resentment returns and you need to remember that marriage was never supposed to become a contest over whose desires matter more.
Send this privately to the couple nobody knows is struggling.

Someone scrolling silently tonight may desperately need permission to stop weaponizing Scripture, stop hiding pain, repent of selfishness, seek healing, and bring Jesus back into the places they stopped talking about.
We support Gospel ministry because grace has already been given to us, not because financial support earns grace from God.
If you want to support the work and go deeper:
But whatever you do after reading this, remember the greater invitation.
No article can forgive your sins.
No ministry can become your Savior.
The One who exposed our sin carried that sin to Calvary.
The One who calls us to repentance also welcomes repentant sinners.
The One who commands husbands and wives to abandon selfishness demonstrated self-giving love with nails through His hands.
And maybe that is the sentence your marriage needs more than any other tonight:
Before asking how much of your spouse belongs to you, remember how completely both of you belong to Christ.
